overview: The Hawaiian Kingdom joined islands with much older political and cultural traditions. Its people developed newspapers, constitutional institutions and international connections while maintaining knowledge of land, water and the arts. This card follows the monarchy from Kamehameha I's consolidation in 1795 to its overthrow in 1893; unification of the principal islands was completed in 1810.

periods.title: A kingdom taking shape
periods.summary: Kamehameha I brought most of the main islands under his rule in 1795. Kauai joined the kingdom in 1810, completing the political unification of the principal islands.

periods.title: Unified royal government
periods.summary: The unified kingdom developed institutions that included the Kuhina Nui, a powerful co-regent from 1819. Lahaina became the capital in 1820, and Hawaiian-language newspaper publication began in 1834.

periods.title: Constitutional government and a growing press
periods.summary: The 1840 constitution established a legislature with nobles and representatives. Hawaiian newspapers, the expanding plantation economy and royal cultural institutions shaped a changing society.

periods.title: A monarchy under pressure
periods.summary: Kalakaua signed the 1887 constitution under duress, losing power as many Native Hawaiians lost political rights. Liliuokalani succeeded him in 1891 and sought to restore the monarchy's authority.

items.text: At Heeia, parallel basalt walls packed mainly with coral slowed the movement of water. Sluice gates controlled freshwater and seawater flows, maintaining brackish conditions in which algae could feed herbivorous fish. This engineering tradition long predates the unified kingdom.

Fishponds helped maintain a food supply when rough seas interrupted ocean fishing. Heeia remained part of the kingdom's lived landscape: Abner Paki received much of the surrounding land during the Mahele of 1848.

Ka Lama Hawaii began publication at Lahainaluna Seminary on Maui in 1834. Surviving issues preserve Hawaiian-language writing from the kingdom itself, giving readers access to contemporary voices alongside later histories.

A letter from Hanalei printed in Ka Hae Hawaii on 14 January 1857 set out Hawaiian month names and day counts. Its author, J. W. Q. Kaia, worried that younger readers no longer knew them. The museum cautions that month names varied between islands.

A surviving Ka Nupepa Kuokoa issue displays the Hawaiian flag in color on 1 January 1862. The original held at Hamilton Library is evidence of printing and national expression that can be lost in poor reproductions; conservation and digitization make such details easier to study.

The Kuhina Nui shared governing authority with the monarch, including land distribution, treaties and justice. Women of high chiefly rank held the office first. Calling it simply a prime ministership understates the authority of these early co-regents.

The constitution of 1840 provided for a council of nobles and a representative body chosen by the people. Early legislative rules developed over time; a written constitution did not immediately create equal political power for everyone.

Lahaina linked local households with visiting whaling ships, trade and, later, sugar plantations. From the 1850s Chinese immigrants worked under plantation contracts, and some settled on Maui after those contracts ended. The kingdom's economic history includes these workers as well as its rulers.

sections.title: Arts, education and the royal court

items.text: Completed in 1882, Iolani Palace combined a royal home with rooms for official receptions and visiting dignitaries. Hula performances and grand balls formed part of its public and ceremonial life.
Liliuokalani composed Aloha Oe in 1878, before becoming queen. Her work as a composer forms part of a larger musical legacy remembered alongside her political life.
In 1886 Liliuokalani founded an educational society to support schooling for Hawaiian girls with limited means. Her public work connected royal patronage with access to education beyond the court.

The Highways Act of 1892 protected public trails and rights of access. Its continuing importance to Hawaiian trail preservation shows how a kingdom-era law can shape the landscape after a change of government.
A royalist attempt to restore Liliuokalani in 1895 failed. She was tried in the palace throne room and confined in an upstairs room, turning the royal residence into a place of imprisonment.
Hawaiians organized petitions against annexation in 1897, and Liliuokalani continued to protest. These records preserve organized political opposition after the monarchy had been overthrown.
Congress passed its annexation resolution on 7 July 1898. This later US action must be distinguished from the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893.

ending.text: On 17 January 1893, the Committee of Safety overthrew Liliuokalani with support from the US minister and US Marines, establishing a Provisional Government. A republic followed in 1894. The removal of the monarchy did not end Hawaiian people, culture or opposition to annexation.
